assumptions: The venture does not take custody, transport, or treat regulated waste unless every required Polish authorization is independently verified.
The family installer participates only through an explicit ordinary commercial agreement and supplies no confidential or unconsented data.
Unit economics are evaluated separately for each equipment state and legal lane.
Licensed downstream operators can provide acceptance and settlement records suitable for the proposed chain of custody.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A specialist Polish waste-role opinion, signed handler pricing and acceptance terms, documented title flows, and a meaningful pilot showing units per stop, rejection rate, full cost per accepted unit, settlement time, payer retention, and positive contribution would justify a higher score.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The proposal correctly separates ownership, waste classification, chain-of-custody information, and routing from physical treatment, letting the venture monetize the handoff without assuming it can freely resell or transport removed equipment. That is a thoughtful mechanism around a messy replacement-job decision.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Every removed covered unit creates a real disposition and compliance event, and stockpiles, rejected loads, or disposal trips can impose measurable costs. The payer varies by equipment and legal lane, and the packet shows no repeatable contract or proof that installers will pay when producer-responsibility schemes may collect for free.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Prepaid routing fees and delegated logistics can limit working-capital exposure, but the proposed 40-300 PLN fee and recovery share are unsupported. Pickup density, packaging, inspection, rejections, licensed-handler fees, and negative-value units can overwhelm revenue, so positive contribution is not yet demonstrated for any lane.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Renewable-equipment replacement should produce a growing stream of disposition events, and one consenting installer offers a practical local workflow test. The packet combines panels, inverters, batteries, and controls whose classifications and economics differ, and it has not established sufficient unit density in a single Polish postcode and equipment class.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Transparent multi-brand routing and better rejection avoidance may help fragmented installers, but producer schemes, wholesalers, and licensed handlers can offer their own traceability or free pickup. Nonexclusive and replaceable access provides no current basis for dominating a lane.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven route could expand across equipment classes, installer networks, repairers, compliance schemes, regions, and lawful reuse markets. Each expansion adds classification and logistics complexity, so the model must prove lane-by-lane economics rather than assume a common marketplace.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Disposition outcomes by model, fault, age, and geography could improve routing values and reduce rejection rates, and operational trust can accumulate. The relevant partners are replaceable, the agreements are nonexclusive, and incumbents may possess superior volume and compliance data.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: The founder has a lawful installer relationship for process discovery and a data-oriented approach suited to routing economics. That relationship conveys no title, customer ownership, regulated permissions, or exclusive flow, so it is a testing advantage rather than a durable commercial one.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: PV panels are within the WEEE regime and an aging installed base should increase replacement and compliance needs. The packet does not establish when local volumes become dense enough or whether existing producer-responsibility collection will absorb most attractive units.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The replacement job is the correct moment to capture disposition information, and installers are a concentrated repeat channel. Only a possible family-firm test is currently accessible; scaling requires simultaneous recruitment of unrelated installers and multiple licensed downstream counterparties.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Keeping transport and treatment with licensed operators is an important boundary, but mistakes in title, waste status, documentation, or role classification can create environmental liability. Low route density and equipment-specific rules add substantial operational risk within the stated time and capital constraints.

highest_value_structural_change: Restrict launch to one equipment class in one dense region under signed installer and licensed-handler agreements, require prepaid or guaranteed lane economics, and exclude every unit whose title, waste classification, or downstream acceptance is not resolved before pickup.
main_structural_strength: The venture targets the exact replacement-job handoff where title, waste status, and downstream route must be resolved, while deliberately separating the information and settlement layer from regulated physical treatment.
primary_score_limiter: No equipment lane has a demonstrated payer and positive fully loaded per-unit economics after collection density, inspection, rejection, packaging, licensed handling, and compliance costs.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Producer-responsibility schemes may already provide simpler or free compliant pickup, and many removed components may have zero or negative recovery value after transport and inspection, eliminating both fee willingness and recovery share.
